reviewer.name: Claude Sonnet, fresh subagent (cold reader 2)
reviewer.origin: Claude Agent tool subagent, model sonnet, a fresh context with only this brief and its files, launched 2026-10-26 by session_01Mxpoi6tFT3FgKmBvtGjRtS (the writer's session)

evidence: Judged the draft “And then read it out loud as you write it. Long, elegant sentences are NOT going to help you when you’re trying to induce. It’s all soup to you at that point.” against SOURCE.txt (replaced words “Read it out loud as you're writing it. Long, elegant sentences don't read well when you're being induced. It's all just soup.”; meaning to keep, from his published guide: “then read the script aloud; long elegant sentences become soup during an induction”) and in the last paragraph of the section. Change check: the_change says Emulate's three sentences (sample cn) replace the three source sentences. DRAFT.txt is those three; they appear once at the end of the third paragraph in CONTEXT.txt, the replaced words are gone, and no AI-writer fix is claimed or visible. CONTEXT.txt is shared with S21 and also holds that draft's sentence; I judged only this draft. Meaning: reading the script aloud while writing is kept. “Long elegant sentences become soup during an induction” is kept across the last two sentences (“NOT going to help you when you're trying to induce” and “It's all soup to you at that point”, where “at that point” is the induction). Two wording drifts, neither a new claim: “being induced” becomes “trying to induce” (the inducer's side instead of the receiver's; in a self-hypnosis guide, in a paragraph about writing your own script, you are both, and the next sentence's “to you” gives the receiver's side), and “don't read well” becomes “are NOT going to help you” (a usefulness claim for a readability claim, but the soup sentence restores the readability point). “trying to induce” uses “induce” without an object, which reads like hypnotist shorthand and is understandable in a section about one trance and one's own induction. No fact, condition, step, safety rule or number is added. Seam and voice: the first sentence follows “...and how you're going to transition between ideas.” as a plain next step, and “And then” is a spoken sequence cue in the same casual register (“whatever”, “just do one”); no hedge, no tidy summary. “NOT” in capitals is the only all-caps word in the section and a notch more emphatic than its neighbours, but emphatic caps are normal in casual advice and it carries a real stance (a flat warning), so I read it as a voice choice the author will see, not a seam. One mechanical mismatch, not a ground for the verdict: the draft's apostrophes are curly (you’re, It’s) while every other sentence in this paragraph and in the first two paragraphs uses straight ones; it shows only in the raw text, but it should be made consistent where the sentences are put in. Tell rows: I went through T01 to T29 and C01 to C04 on the draft in context. T20 is the one row I find happening: the paragraph ends on a short colloquial punch line (the linter's B7). I judge it justified here because “soup” is the required meaning from his published guide, the line sits in the slot of the approved “It's all just soup.”, it adds the reason (the sentences blur) instead of summing the paragraph up or moralising, and “at that point” places it in the induction. T29 considered and not happening for the same reason (dropping the line would lose “soup” from the meaning to keep; it is a new consideration, not a restatement or a moral). Weighed and found absent: T02 (the paragraph is four short pieces of advice in a row, but the first is a long list sentence, the last two carry stance and a joke, and the draft is the same trio of jobs as the words it replaces, so it adds no cadence); T15 (the draft is a sentence-for-sentence rewording by design, but the swaps change register and construction rather than putting rarer words in, and nothing is a synonym swap for its own sake); T07 (“And then” orders the steps and the caps carry a warning, so neither is stage-direction filler); T22 and T10 (a blunt warning, no reassurance or permission formula); T08 (the image comes last and nothing explains it); T16 and T18 (no negative reveal or flip); T26 (write/writing repeats the sentence before, as the old text did); T13 and T09 (the soup image and the caps are noticing, and the last line gets more attention than its information, not equal weight); C02 (“it” is the script, with “this” in the sentence before; “that point” is the induction in the sentence before; “this” has no earlier anchor in the context, but that is outside the draft and unchanged); C03 and C04 none. Linter B7 “short landing at paragraph end”: accepted, for the reasons given under T20. Linter D9 “follows the source order”: accepted; the three sentences are rewritten in place, so 1/1 agreement is by construction, and the T13 and T09 checks it asks for came out absent as above. Linter E36/E41 “heavy second person”: accepted; 12.5 per 100 is four “you” in 32 words, a little denser than the paragraph's own first sentence (three in 30 words, 10.0) and close to the paragraph as a whole (seven in 62 words, 11.3), and “you” is the person writing the script and going into the trance, as across the whole guide. The draft has two more “you” than the old words (“help you”, “to you at that point”), both idiomatic, and the voice is a blunt warning, not the calm validating coach register E41 targets. One note on the writer's ledger: its T14 and T15 lines say the draft puts back a point Emulate dropped; here all three sentences are Emulate's own, so that wording does not apply, but it changes no judgment.
